review: This is a really deep game, in spite of my initial impressions. I've had it on my iPad for a year or so, but finally invested some time in it, and really enjoying it. I still don't have a handle on all the factors and large-scale dice rolls, but can see my knowledge will grow. So now I've bought it on Steam and play on both platforms - iPad when I want something to play anywhere, Steam/Windows when I want to work with some of the mods like Fly Casual (sort of a Firefly experience). I can't see me growing tired of this game for a long time, if ever.

There's a good game here, but it's buried under an endless mound of data. For each game you need to keep track of dozens of crew including jobs (for your captain and officers) and talents for each job. Each crew member also wears gear so you have to decide what weapons and armor you want each to use. And finally you have ships with dozens of modules of build slots that can each be filled lots of different modules and each module come in muliple different modules and levels. And that's the challenge for me. In order to really play this game well you need spreadsheets and notes and probably many hours of theory crafting or reading guides etc. I like the depth and the amount of data points, but there has to be a way to make it easier for the player to manage. I found the constant management of all the individual things that need to be managed along with a bit too much RNG in the card games became tedious for me. Your mileage may vary. I am reluctantly giving it a thumbs down, not because there's not a good game here - there is - but rather because it just wasn't fun enough for me to keep playing it.
It's a good game, and they deserve a thumbs up just from the sheer amount of content updates they continue to put out.

Deep, expansive, and genuinely engaging.

Star Traders: Frontiers makes a great first impression – and that impression only grows over time. After a few hours of play, I feel like I've barely scratched the surface of 1% of what this game has to offer. That's both fascinating and a little overwhelming – in the best possible way.

The biggest highlight is the thoughtfully designed character training and progression system, woven together with story-driven adventures. The RPG layer here is genuinely solid – the variety of professions and career paths is impressive, and every decision regarding your crew and captain carries real consequences.

A pleasant surprise is also the learning curve – the game doesn't throw a tutorial manual in your face, but you can comfortably learn on the fly, make mistakes, and rely on save states. It's an approach I really appreciate.

If I had one criticism, it would be the occasionally lengthy dialogues and demanding English – for players without fluent language skills, it can be a slight barrier. But that's more of a side effect of a richly built world than an actual flaw.

Recommended for anyone looking for a game with real depth, who isn't afraid to invest time in learning its mechanics.

This game does something that no other game is doing for space sims. It creates a living universe with actors who have agency, resulting in emergent gameplay which builds excellent stories in a living, breathing universe, which has enormous replayability. You can play in many different ways and all the many occupations have paths to success; the game rewards experimentation, thought and risk taking.

The contacts system alone is genius, and maybe is only matched by Crusader Kings 2. The mission system is excellent and actually has consequences for success and failure, and usually also has time penalties for not completing actions in good time. Combat is difficult and often unpredictable, like real life, and often the best course is to run. It is a rpg at it's core but many of it's systems attempt to be realistic simulations. People complaining about RNG in reviews do not get this! The die roll/RNG system is also hugely innovative. It gives players the ability to influence the outcome without knowing exactly how the percentage chance of success/failure is derived, which creates important decision points for the player in everything they do - there is risk and reward in every action.

To get the most from Star Traders (and it has a huge amount to offer) you need to accept that the learning curve is huge and the tutorial can only take you so far. You will need to do a little research online but there are many excellent player and Trese brother resources available to help you. I suggest you pick an occupation that appeals (you can't go wrong with Explorer!) and look up some builds and basic strategies and dive in. You will not be doing a single play through...

You need to accept graphics may not be the best but they are very functional (have you played Battle Brothers?), and the ship designs are good and you get used to them. Trese brothers are a small (but growing) independent developer making games they love to play themselves. Each new game has got better and better, and have always been super well supported. The level of support for their games is probably more than any other developer I am aware off (and I play No Man's Sky). They have up dated the game regularly for years after launch based on feedback from the very culty and obsessive community, and they are very active with the community. Their latest game is very good, they have delved into 3D graphics and I hope that one day they remake Star Traders with better visuals!

You also need to accept and enjoy the difficulty and RNG because that is the point... but remember that because of the all the updates game balance is excellent, and there is always a successful strategy. Star Sector is great but it does not have the depth of this.

So in short this is not a pick up and play game (at least not in the beginning). You need to commit some time and effort but if you do it will pay back immeasurably!

Star Traders: Frontiers is already the closest I’ve come on PC to recapturing the feel of a classic Traveller campaign, even with only a handful of hours in. I’m still very much learning the systems, but it’s clear this is a deep, flexible space RPG rather than a shallow “checklist” game.

What I’ve enjoyed so far is how many different roles the game clearly supports: trader, bounty hunter, pirate, explorer, spy, or something in between, and you feel that from the very first captain you create. Even in my short time, picking a background, ship, and crew already feels like choosing the style of campaign I want to play, not just tweaking stats. The turn-based ship and crew combat, the event tests, and the faction politics together give it that “tabletop session in a box” vibe that Traveller fans will recognize.

I also appreciate that there are a lot of difficulty and customization options, which makes it easier to dial things in while you’re still climbing the learning curve. The game can absolutely be punishing and a bit overwhelming at first, but that seems to be the trade-off for having so many interconnected systems and meaningful decisions. So far, I’ve found that taking it slow, focusing on a simple role, and accepting a few early mistakes makes the whole experience much more enjoyable than trying to “solve” it on the first run.

Even this early on, though, Star Traders: Frontiers already feels like a game I could sink a lot of time into as I get more comfortable with its mechanics. If you’re interested in a crunchy, sandboxy space RPG with real consequences and the freedom to chart your own course, it’s absolutely worth a look—especially if you’ve ever wanted a Traveller-style experience on PC.

Star Traders: Frontiers, developed and published by Trese Brothers, is an expansive spacefaring RPG that blends open-ended sandbox gameplay with strategic management, narrative choices, and tactical combat. Set in a procedurally generated universe shaped by rival factions and shifting political tensions, the game places players in the role of a starship captain attempting to carve out a legacy among the stars. Rather than guiding players through a strictly scripted story, the game offers an open galaxy filled with opportunities and dangers, allowing each captain’s career to develop organically through personal decisions and the unpredictable events of the universe. This design gives Star Traders: Frontiers a unique sense of freedom, encouraging players to experiment with different career paths while navigating complex interstellar politics.

From the beginning, players create their captain by selecting attributes, skills, and a starting profession, which helps determine their early gameplay style. Some captains may begin as traders moving valuable goods between planets to accumulate wealth, while others may pursue more dangerous professions such as bounty hunting, espionage, piracy, or exploration. Each approach shapes the way players interact with the galaxy’s factions, which include powerful houses and independent groups constantly competing for influence. Accepting missions, transporting cargo, or assisting certain factions can strengthen alliances while damaging relations with their rivals. These shifting political dynamics add an ongoing layer of tension and strategy, forcing players to carefully consider how their actions affect long-term relationships.

A defining feature of the game is its intricate crew management system. A starship is far more than a vehicle—it is a small community filled with specialists whose abilities determine whether missions succeed or fail. Crew members occupy specific roles such as engineers, navigators, medics, spies, and soldiers, each contributing unique talents that affect ship performance and survival during dangerous encounters. Officers serve as elite members of the crew with multiple professions and powerful abilities, allowing players to build highly specialized teams suited for combat, exploration, or diplomacy. Maintaining morale is equally important, as unhappy crew members may abandon ship or cause problems if their needs are ignored. Balancing salaries, promotions, and mission risk becomes an essential part of managing a successful crew.

Combat in Star Traders: Frontiers occurs both in space and during boarding or ground encounters, offering a layered tactical experience. Ship combat is turn-based and involves maneuvering your vessel, managing weapon systems, and coordinating crew talents to outmaneuver opponents. Battles can involve pirates, rival faction ships, or hostile forces encountered during missions, and victory often requires careful planning rather than brute force. Boarding actions transition into tactical crew combat where small teams engage enemies using specialized skills and positioning. Soldiers, commanders, and other combat professions bring unique abilities to these encounters, making team composition an important strategic consideration. This dual combat system ensures that encounters remain varied and engaging throughout the campaign.

The game’s economy and exploration systems add even more depth to the experience. Players can profit from trading commodities across star systems, discovering lucrative trade routes, or exploiting shortages created by political conflicts. Exploration missions may uncover rare resources, hidden dangers, or valuable information that can be sold to interested factions. Random events, rumors, and mission opportunities constantly appear as players travel, giving the galaxy a sense of life and unpredictability. Because the universe is procedurally generated, every playthrough presents different opportunities, encouraging repeated campaigns with new strategies and character builds.

Visually, Star Traders: Frontiers adopts a stylized 2D presentation that emphasizes atmosphere and readability rather than high-end graphical spectacle. Character portraits, ship designs, and planetary environments feature detailed artwork that captures the tone of a gritty science-fiction frontier. The interface contains a large number of menus and information panels, reflecting the game’s enormous mechanical depth. While this can initially feel overwhelming, players who invest the time to understand the systems will discover an incredibly detailed simulation where nearly every decision has meaningful consequences.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its remarkable replayability. With multiple captain backgrounds, ship types, faction alliances, and strategic playstyles available, no two campaigns unfold in exactly the same way. A player might begin as a humble merchant only to become a feared pirate lord, or serve as a loyal agent of a powerful faction shaping the balance of power across the sector. The procedural galaxy, evolving political conflicts, and flexible career options combine to create an experience that constantly generates new stories.

Despite its many strengths, Star Traders: Frontiers does have a steep learning curve that may intimidate newcomers. The number of mechanics governing ship systems, crew talents, faction reputation, and economic management can be daunting during the early hours of play. However, players who enjoy deep strategy games and detailed simulations will likely find this complexity to be one of the game’s most rewarding aspects. The sense of mastery that develops as players learn to navigate the galaxy’s systems is deeply satisfying and encourages long-term engagement.

Overall, Star Traders: Frontiers stands as one of the most ambitious indie space RPGs available on Steam. Its blend of tactical combat, role-playing choices, strategic management, and dynamic storytelling creates a richly layered experience that rewards patience and experimentation. For players who enjoy sandbox RPGs with meaningful freedom and depth, the game offers countless hours of exploration and emergent narrative.

Star Traders: Frontiers stands out because its systems genuinely interlock, with factions, politics, trade, and conflict evolving dynamically and responding to player decisions in meaningful, long-term ways. Deep character and crew progression, combined with turn-based planning and real consequences for mistakes, creates a rare single-player sandbox strategy RPG where foresight and systemic understanding matter more than execution or spectacle.

I don't think I can imagine a better game for what this sets out to be. You can play it as an in-depth and demanding rpg where every decision matters, or you can change the settings and have a semi-idle crew management adventure to play while you're watching a favorite show or listening to an audiobook. Build-crafting can't really describe what goes into shaping your crew, ship, and captain in this game: you choose the game you want to play by choosing and developing these components. I really could not give this game higher praise, except to mention that the dev team has put out a patch every few days since its release -- including what would be many DLCs worth of content in any other game for free. One of my all-time favorites up there with Baldur's Gate II and Mount and Blade Warband!

[h1]Star Traders: Competence is Dangerous[/h1]

[b]Star Traders is fully functional, endlessly playable, and—horrifyingly—the devs [i]actually made it fun.[/i][/b]

I know, it’s shocking. A game that launches finished, balanced, and with meaningful updates? Someone call the authorities.

[h2]Gameplay That Actually Works (Suspiciously So)[/h2]

In Star Traders, you can:

[list]
[*]Command ships, trade goods, and explore the galaxy without immediately crashing the game,
[*]Engage in tense combat and make strategic decisions that actually matter,
[*]Manage crew and resources in ways that are satisfying instead of just tedious busywork, and
[*]Customize your fleet without being forced into $20 DLC for the “Advanced Warp Drive Skin Pack”.
[/list]

It’s weirdly addictive. Every decision feels impactful, every trade route carefully considered, and the risk/reward balance actually works. I keep finding myself saying, “just one more jump… maybe one more mission…” for hours on end.

[h2]Updates That Should Be Illegal[/h2]

As if the gameplay weren’t already terrifyingly well done, the devs continue to patch and improve it. Free updates keep adding content, balancing mechanics, and making the game more fun, which is basically criminal in today’s gaming climate.

[code]
Update #???:

Added new missions and factions

Balanced combat for more tactical depth

Improved trading mechanics to make profits satisfyingly dangerous

Continued the absurd act of respecting players
[/code]

I’m starting to think the Trese Brothers run on some sort of forbidden developer magic, probably just coffee, but you never know...

[h2]Why This is Fun (and a Little Scary)[/h2]

Star Traders manages to combine:

[list]
[*]Exploration — the galaxy actually feels vast, alive, and full of secrets,
[*]Trading — risk versus reward feels real, and profitable routes are genuinely satisfying,
[*]Combat — tactical and challenging without ever feeling unfair, and
[*]Progression — leveling your crew and fleet feels meaningful.
[/list]

It’s the perfect mix of strategy, RPG, and space adventure. And somehow it all works without microtransactions or punishing design.

[h2]A Warning to the Industry[/h2]

If the Trese Brothers keep this up, we may see:

[list]
[*]Other games launching finished,
[*]Developers who actually care,
[*]Players expecting fun instead of frustration, and
[*]An unstoppable wave of professionalism sweeping across the galaxy.
[/list]

Truly terrifying.

This has been an interesting experience for me as I haven't often played card based games.   Star Traders does an good job of balancing the RNG elements with the options presented by the cards, with allowances for special skills your captain and crew can develop.   You don't build a "deck" per se, but your crew and equipment does influence the outcomes of each encounter.

There is an overarching story line with multiple plot threads you can choose to follow.   You'll need multiple run-throughs to complete the various endings and you won't be able to complete everything in a single run.   There are also a variety of side missions, quests, and general activities you can perform (trading, raiding, patrolling, etc.) although you'll get plenty of that accepting various radiant missions.

Factions, Changing Alliances, Crew Building, Ship Building, Storyline & Missions, and some resource management all layer in to a fairly complex game.   You'll probably find the biggest constraint to be time.   Missions have deadlines and travel, landings, repair, combat, and most activities take time to complete.   If you're not careful you'll find you're missing deadlines or having to choose which missions to complete.   But selecting a handful of missions in the same system (or along the same travel path) can increase your efficiency greatly.

Character equipment seems to be where the game is the weakest.   The options there are limited and heavily influenced by the armory you buy (or equip) in your ship.   You can take 4 of your crew into battle and they have a limited number of slots for gear, and variations of skills and moves they can perform based on their class, level, and what they were trained in.   You'll have to deal with a LOT of ground combat so best be prepared.   There are plenty of guides and recommendations on the build-outs, but you'll find your own rhythm and preferences after awhile.

Ships are built upon various chassis with various number of heavy, medium, and light slots available into which you can add in a huge variety of options to configure battleships, carriers, explorers, or whatever mix you want.   There are some mandatory components like engines, bridge, and crew quarters that can be important based on what "size" they are (taking up valuable slots), and everything comes with a price.   The ship options are massively more detailed compared to what's available for the crew and with enough money you can easily configure some super-ships.   Some of the ship chassis easily stand-out from the rest based on number of available slots and cost, and a lot of chassis need to be unlocked through missions or faction reputation.

In any case this is a fun game, can take a bit of time to master, with many options on how to play.   Definitely recommend it.

Trading is similarly deep. profit, legality, and dealing with enemies is much deeper than a surface play indicates. it's good to keep a notepad open to discover profitable routes, and you can't even touch the true profit until you build up enormous faction and pay for trading rights for better goods.

but yes, deep gameplay is concealed by simplistic-looking mechanics, and a lot of people can't see past the surface level to catch the much deeper gameplay. Quests are not always easy, have timers, and faction is a constant balancing act that can only be repaired by extensive work protecting the planets that you may have inadvertently made your enemy.

In short, the game has enormous potential disguised by simplistic-looking mechanics, the quests are often deeply immersive and complex, and you can tell that the dev team spent much more of their effort on making sure that the game and plots themselves were enough to hold attention. If you are looking for a simple space shoot-em-up, you are going to be doomed to disappointment, but the stories and plotlines make Westeros look like a children's story.

In short, if you are more of an intellectual gamer, this game is for you, even though the learning curve LOOKS shallow, even now I am learning more about how deep the plots really go. Sometimes the biggest ships are not the best for your captain and playstyle, and sometimes retreat or surrender is the only sane option.
